extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for evaluating whether a claimed invention satisfies the utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101 (and related 35 U.S.C. 112 considerations), including when an asserted utility is specific, substantial, and credible. Covers examiner procedures, examples, and how therapeutic/research-tool claims are assessed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with 35 U.S.C. 101 — invention must be 'useful'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Office must examine each application to ensure compliance with the 'useful invention' or utility requirement of 35 U.S.C. 101; to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 an applicant must claim statutory subject matter and show that the claimed invention is 'useful' for some purpose either explicitly or implicitly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the overarching requirement. Application of the utility element is the focus of the guidelines. See MPEP § 2107 for detailed examination guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific utility
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'specific utility' is specific to the subject matter claimed and can 'provide a well-defined and particular benefit to the public.' A general statement that a compound 'may be useful' or has 'useful biological properties' is not sufficient to define a specific utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Office personnel should distinguish disclosures that identify a specific use/application from mere indications that the invention 'may prove useful.' Examples of insufficient specificity: treating 'unspecified disorders', calling a polynucleotide simply a 'gene probe' without identifying a DNA target, or broadly alleging 'diagnostic utility' without specifying the condition. Conversely, disclosing a specific biological activity and reasonably correlating it to a disease condition suffices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantial utility
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Substantial' utility requires that an asserted use show the claimed invention has a significant and presently available benefit to the public — an immediate, well-defined, real-world use; utilities that require further research to identify or confirm a real-world context are not 'substantial.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accept reasonable uses that provide public benefit; do not require that products/services be currently available to the public. Examples of non-substantial utilities (require further research): (A) basic research into properties/mechanisms; (B) method of treating an unspecified disease; (C) assay for/identifying material that itself has no specific/substantial utility; (D) method of making a material that itself lacks specific/substantial/credible utility; (E) claim to an intermediate product for making a final product that has no specific/substantial/credible utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Credible utility / not 'incredible'
rubrics_metrics.description: An asserted utility must be credible; an invention that is 'inoperative' (does not operate to produce the claimed results) is not 'useful.' To violate 35 U.S.C. 101, the claimed device must be totally incapable of achieving a useful result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rejections on 'incredible' or 'speculative' utility are rare and fact-specific. Partial success or crude/perfect embodiments do not establish total incapacity; a small degree of utility can be sufficient. Office personnel should not label an asserted utility 'incredible' unless facts clearly support a lack-of-utility rejection. Examples of 'incredible' claims (fact specific): perpetual motion machines, cold fusion, uncharacterized compositions claimed to cure many cancers, methods contradicting known science.

rubrics_metrics.name: Research tools and 'for research purposes' labels
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling an invention as a 'research tool,' 'intermediate' or 'for research purposes' does not determine patent utility; many research tools have clear, specific, and substantial utility (e.g., gas chromatographs, screening assays).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish between inventions that have a specifically identified substantial utility and inventions whose asserted utility requires further research to identify/confirm. The mere fact an invention is used in research does not preclude patentable utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Therapeutic/pharmacological utility standard
rubrics_metrics.description: Therapeutic or pharmacological utilities are judged under the same legal standards as other technologies: showing pharmacological activity typically provides an 'immediate benefit to the public' and satisfies utility requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identification of a pharmacological activity (including in vitro data in appropriate circumstances) can be sufficient to show practical utility. FDA approval is not required; patent-law usefulness is distinct from FDA standards of safety/efficacy. Early-stage evidence (e.g., in vitro, analogy to known active compounds) can suffice; examiners should rely on case law such as Nelson v. Bowler, Cross v. Iizuka, In re Jolles, and In re Brana.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wholly inoperative inventions versus partial success
rubrics_metrics.description: A rejection for lack of utility requires that the invention be 'totally incapable' of producing a useful result; partial success is sufficient to avoid a lack-of-utility rejection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts have held that even crude or imperfect embodiments showing some beneficial function satisfy utility. Rejections based solely on partial failures of embodiments are inappropriate; find lack of utility only when evidence shows total incapacity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relationship between 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deficiency under the utility prong of 35 U.S.C. 101 also creates a deficiency under 35 U.S.C. 112(a) (pre-AIA 112, first paragraph); section 112 presupposes compliance with section 101 as a matter of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an application fails as a matter of fact to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101, it also may fail to enable one of ordinary skill to use the invention under 35 U.S.C. 112(a). A lack-of-utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 should be accompanied by a separate 35 U.S.C. 112(a) rejection that incorporates the factual basis from the 101 rejection. Do not impose a 112(a) lack-of-utility rejection unless a 101 rejection is proper; impose separate rejections for 112 grounds unrelated to utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on the claimed invention and per-claim evaluation
rubrics_metrics.description: The claimed invention (each claim) is the focus of the utility assessment; each claim must be evaluated on its own merits for statutory compliance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dependent claims generally have utility if the independent claim does and both are in the same statutory category, except when the dependent claim specifies a different utility. When a species within a generic claim has established utility, a generic claim covering the genus is generally sufficient unless it can be shown that other species encompassed by the claim lack utility — in which case applicant should be encouraged to amend to exclude non-utility species.

rubrics_metrics.name: One credible asserted utility suffices
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant need only make one credible assertion of specific utility for the claimed invention to satisfy 35 U.S.C. 101 and 35 U.S.C. 112; additional statements of utility, even if not credible, do not render the claimed invention lacking utility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a properly claimed invention meets at least one stated objective, utility is established. Examples/case law: Raytheon v. Roper; In re Gottlieb. Examiners should not penalize inventions for extra non-credible utility statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant statements alone cannot be sole basis for lack of utility rejection
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements made by the applicant in the specification or during prosecution cannot, standing alone, be the basis for a lack-of-utility rejection under 35 U.S.C. 101 or 35 U.S.C. 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applicants may include statements whose technical accuracy is not easily confirmed if those statements are not necessary to establish patentability. Examiners should not require applicants to strike nonessential utility statements, nor should examiners read unclaimed results or limitations into a claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure — determine if asserted or well-established utility exists
rubrics_metrics.description: Upon initial examination, the examiner should review the specification to determine if there are statements asserting that the claimed invention is useful for any particular purpose; a complete disclosure should identify a specific and substantial utility for the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A statement of specific and substantial utility should fully and clearly explain why the applicant believes the invention is useful and enable one ordinarily skilled in the art to understand the belief (e.g., explain purpose or how the invention may be used). If an applicant rebuts a prima facie 101 lack-of-utility rejection satisfactorily, withdraw the 101 rejection and corresponding 112(a) rejection.
